processing: Little is documented under this name. Regional Japanese green tea is typically steamed, rolled and dried; nearby Omogo tea is sold as bancha and oolong too.
harvest_season: Little is documented. Japanese green tea is typically picked from spring, and mountain areas tend to run later.
appearance_dry: As is typical of Japanese regional green tea, dark green rolled leaf.
appearance_liquor: As is typical of Japanese regional green tea, a clear yellow-green.
appearance_wet: As is typical of the class, soft green leaf pieces.
taste_profile: No documented profile exists under this name. Expect a plain, fresh mountain green tea in the general regional style.

brewing.notes: General sencha guidance, as no local method is recorded. If the leaf looks like bancha, use hotter water.

vintage_note: How it is sold is not well recorded. Regional Japanese green tea is usually the current year's harvest, and local bancha is less tied to freshness.
description:
Kuma-cha appears to be a name for tea from the Kuma area of upland Ehime, on Shikoku, now part of Kumakogen town. A search found no page using this exact name, so treat it with caution.

Tea is listed among Kumakogen's local products. The best-described tea from the town is Omogo tea, grown in the Ainomine area above 700 metres, where sellers credit the cool nights for a concentrated flavour. Whether Kuma-cha and Omogo tea overlap is unclear, so do not take them as the same thing.

For tasting, treat it as you would any unfamiliar Japanese regional green: sencha parameters first, then adjust. No taste notes here are specific to this tea.

If you find a bag, the producer's name and the style are what count.
history: Little is documented about Kuma-cha, including when the name came into use or who made it known. Tea has long been grown in the mountains of Kumakogen, as the account of Omogo tea suggests, but the link to this name is not established.
